name: Infrared Spectroscopy
what: Infrared (IR) spectroscopy identifies the types of chemical bonds present in a molecule by measuring which wavelengths of infrared radiation are absorbed. The spectrum is displayed as transmittance (%) versus wavenumber (cm-1), with absorption appearing as downward troughs.
why: IR spectroscopy is widely used to identify functional groups in organic compounds, confirm the purity of synthesised products, and detect substances in forensic and environmental analysis. It is a fast, non-destructive technique that provides clear evidence for the presence or absence of specific bond types.

items.title: I can describe the principle of infrared spectroscopy
items.what: Different chemical bonds absorb infrared radiation at characteristic frequencies (wavenumbers). When IR radiation is passed through a sample, bonds absorb energy at their specific frequencies and vibrate more, and the absorbed frequencies appear as troughs (low transmittance) in the resulting spectrum.
items.why: Understanding the principle explains why different functional groups appear at predictable positions in the spectrum, making it possible to use wavenumber tables to identify bond types systematically.
items.example: The O-H bond in an alcohol absorbs IR radiation strongly in the range 3200-3600 cm-1. When ethanol is analysed, a broad trough appears in this region, confirming the presence of a hydroxyl group.

items.title: I can identify bond types present in a sample from given infrared spectroscopy data
items.what: By comparing the wavenumber positions of absorption troughs in a spectrum against a reference table of characteristic absorption ranges, you can identify which bond types are present. The absence of a trough in a particular range can also rule out certain functional groups.
items.why: Identifying bond types from IR data is a core analytical skill that provides direct evidence for the functional groups in a molecule, which in turn constrains what the compound can and cannot be.
items.example: An IR spectrum shows troughs at approximately 2950 cm-1 (C-H bond, 2850-3090 cm-1) and 1735 cm-1 (C=O bond, consistent with an ester at 1720-1840 cm-1), but no broad trough at 2500-3500 cm-1, ruling out a carboxylic acid O-H.

items.title: I can determine the identity of organic compounds from provided options using given infrared spectroscopy data
items.what: When given a set of possible compounds and an IR spectrum, you eliminate candidates by checking which bond types should be present or absent. The compound whose expected absorption pattern matches the observed spectrum is the correct identification.
items.why: This is a key exam skill in VCE Chemistry. The process of elimination using IR data, particularly using the absence of expected peaks, is often more decisive than confirming peaks that may overlap.
items.example: A compound with formula C4H8O2 shows a C=O trough at 1740 cm-1 but no broad O-H trough at 2500-3500 cm-1. This rules out a carboxylic acid and confirms it is an ester, since esters have C=O (1720-1840 cm-1) but no O-H absorption.

items.title: I can explain the role of the fingerprint region in IR spectroscopy
items.what: The fingerprint region spans 500-1500 cm-1 and contains a complex, unique pattern of absorption bands resulting from the combined vibrations of all atoms in the molecule. Like a human fingerprint, it is unique to each compound.
items.why: The fingerprint region is used as a confirmatory test to verify the identity of a compound by comparing its spectrum with a reference library spectrum. It is especially useful when functional group analysis alone is insufficient to distinguish between similar compounds.
items.example: Two different isomers may both show C=O and C-H absorptions in the functional group region, but their fingerprint regions (500-1500 cm-1) will differ, allowing them to be distinguished when compared against known reference spectra.
